item.title: Denmark Says Russian Warship Fired Flares at Military Helicopter
item.description:
Denmark’s foreign minister announced on Tuesday that he had summoned Russia’s ambassador after Denmark’s military said a Russian frigate fired two flares at a Danish air force helicopter the previous day. One flare passed close to the helicopter, the Danish military said in a statement.

The incident came as tensions between Russia and NATO countries in Europe were running high over a string of airspace incursions by Russian jets and drones, as well as sabotage plots and attacks that European officials have blamed Russia for.

European leaders have accused Russia of trying to provoke and destabilize countries supporting Ukraine as the war there grinds toward another bloody winter, over four years after Russia’s full-scale invasion.

The military said in its statement that the flares flew as a Danish air force helicopter was conducting “routine photographic coverage of a Russian frigate” in international waters off the coast of southern Denmark.

“This is completely unacceptable,” Lars Lokke Rasmussen, Denmark’s foreign minister, said in a statement that the Foreign Ministry released on social media.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Denmark called the move “reckless action” by Russia.

“Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide,” she said in a statement her office shared on social media. “They will not succeed. We will not waver.”

Vladimir Barbin, the Russian ambassador to Denmark, said in a statement that Russia would “thoroughly investigate all the circumstances of the incident” even as he accused the Danish military of regularly carrying out “dangerous maneuvers” near Russian warships.

The incident came a day after a Russian strike on a Ukrainian train station near the Polish border where David Petraeus, the former C.I.A. director, was traveling on a train. Another train had just left the station with the former British prime minister Boris Johnson and other European politicians and diplomats.

Countries neighboring Russia and Ukraine have also been plagued in recent months by drone incursions as the war in Ukraine spills over their borders.

On Tuesday, President Gitanas Nauseda of Lithuania said that NATO fighter jets had destroyed a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace overnight. He thanked allies for their response.

“With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region,” he said on social media, although he did not say what country the drone belonged to.

On Monday, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, the Polish defense minister, said on social media that the Polish military had recovered a drone from the Baltic Sea and that early indications suggested that it had come from Russia.

item.title: Houthis Report Deadly Saudi Airstrikes as Kingdom Issues Mass Alerts
item.description:
Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen on Tuesday accused each other of launching attacks at their territories, with reports of casualties on both sides, days after the Iran-backed militia seized key areas of Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

A Saudi military spokesman, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said that the Houthis had targeted three cities across the kingdom, injuring 13 people, without specifying when the attacks happened. The Houthis have not commented publicly on those attacks.

Also on Tuesday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, said in a statement that Saudi airstrikes had killed three people, including two children, in Taiz province. The Saudi government did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the strikes.

The Saudi Civil Defense issued emergency alerts overnight in several cities on the country’s western coast, including Jeddah, Yanbu and Taif, and issued additional emergency alerts on Tuesday afternoon for Mecca, Jeddah and Taif.

The alerts on Tuesday were the most widespread across the kingdom in a single day since the fighting in Yemen intensified. An attack on Jeddah would be a notable escalation, because Saudi Arabia’s crown prince has been working out of that city in recent days. He held a cabinet meeting there on Tuesday with other senior officials.

Saudi Arabia leads a military coalition in Yemen that has been fighting to restore the country’s internationally-recognized government since 2015, after the Houthis seized control of the capital, Sanaa. A truce in 2022 largely quelled the fighting but has unraveled in recent weeks, with fierce ground clashes between Houthi fighters and forces allied with the Saudi-backed government.

The full scope of ground fighting remains unclear but the hostilities have displaced approximately 125,000 people in Yemen since September, according to the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

In recent days, the Houthis have seized control of territory along the Red Sea, including the port city of Mokha and Perim Island, which sits in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the sea’s southern entrance.

The Houthi advance on the coast of the Red Sea is a major setback for Saudi Arabia, which has pivoted to exporting most of its oil through there after Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf in the early days of the war with the United States.

The Houthis have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping and attacked vessels in the Red Sea and oil facilities in the kingdom. Analysts say that the capture of Perim Island could give the Houthis a strategic foothold to further threaten shipping. The Houthis have denied posing any threat to maritime security and say they are only targeting Saudi Arabia.

On Friday, Saudi authorities were forced to shut down their East-West oil pipeline, a critical conduit for getting oil to the country’s Red Sea ports, following a drone attack they said was launched from Iraq.

No group has officially claimed the drone attack on the East-West pipeline, although on Saturday President Trump said Iran was “probably” behind the assault. Iran has not commented on the claim.

Saudi officials have said the drone came from Iraq, which has been a hotbed for well-armed militias under Tehran’s sway that the Iraqi government has struggled to bring under control.

As the war between the United States and Iran drags on, Saudi Arabia has increasingly found itself caught in the middle. The kingdom recently asked the United States to take military action against the Houthis but was rebuffed by Mr. Trump, according to officials with knowledge of the conversations.

With limited options for how to respond, Saudi Arabia is likely to turn to direct engagement with Iran to try to ease tensions, some analysts say.

Despite the ongoing tensions, diplomatic relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran — which were restored in 2023 under a deal brokered by China — have not been cut. Even as the kingdom was on alert for attacks from Yemen, Iran’s minister of science, research and technology, Hossein Saraf, visited Riyadh on Tuesday for a conference on artificial intelligence.

The U.N. Security Council on Tuesday held an emergency meeting about the situation in Yemen, focusing on the Houthi advances and threat to global shipping and energy supplies. Diplomats called for the resumption of negotiations to defuse the conflict.

“The impact of these hostilities also extends to the civilian population, forcing people to flee their homes, causing civilian casualties and putting already stretched humanitarian operations under growing pressure,” said Khaled Khiari, the U.N.’s top official for the Middle East.

Amid the turmoil, Mr. Trump on Monday nominated Representative Wesley Hunt of Texas to serve as U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, filling a post that had remained vacant since January 2025. Mr. Hunt, a retired U.S. Army captain, previously served in Saudi Arabia as a diplomatic liaison officer.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia, the kingdom’s de facto ruler, traveled to Egypt on Tuesday to meet the country’s leader, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, to “discuss ways to enhance fraternal bilateral relations and issues of mutual concern,” according to the state-run Saudi Press Agency.

The visit to Cairo comes a day after the crown prince met with Adm. Brad Cooper, who oversees U.S. operations in the Middle East, in the Saudi coastal city of Jeddah, to discuss “the latest regional developments.”

Farnaz Fassihi in New York contributed reporting.

item.title: Israeli Strikes in Gaza Kill Teenager and Civil Defense Worker, Local Official Says
item.description:
Israeli airstrikes in a residential Gaza neighborhood on Tuesday killed a teenager and a civil defense worker, according to a local official, amid mounting international pressure on Israel to halt its attacks in the enclave.

The Israeli military said that it had “directed an attack against Hamas terrorists” and that the outcome in the Gaza City attack was “under review.” The Israeli operation in Gaza followed strikes in the past day that the military said had killed Hamas militants.

On Tuesday, an Israeli drone strike in the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood of Gaza City killed a teenager, identified as Mohammed al-Zinati, 15, and wounded other people, a member of the civil defense team, Motaz Ayyoub, said in a phone interview.

A second drone strike less than a minute later killed Sharif Labad, a civil defense worker who was not on duty but had rushed to the scene, Mr. Ayyoub said. He said that he and Mr. Labad had been planning to meet and attend a wedding when his friend responded to the earlier strike.

“We are now in the mosque to do the funeral prayer,” Mr. Ayyoub said.

In separate statements on Tuesday, the Israeli military said that it had killed a Hamas commander in the northern Gaza Strip overnight and that it had killed two Hamas operatives on Monday, one in the Khan Younis area in southern Gaza and another in Gaza City.

Late on Tuesday, the Israeli military also said it struck “a senior Hamas terrorist” in the southern Gaza Strip. The office of Israel’s prime minister and minister of defense said in a joint statement that the strike had targeted the commander of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade and vowed that “Hamas will not remain in Gaza.”

Israel has continued to carry out deadly strikes in Gaza over the past six weeks, despite efforts by President Trump’s Board of Peace to halt the attacks following its announcement in late July that Hamas had agreed to surrender its weapons. Under the disarmament framework, Israel was expected to halt its military operations in Gaza except in cases of immediate self-defense, but Israeli officials rejected the agreement.

A senior Board of Peace official recently criticized Israel’s continuing strikes during a speech at the United Nations, saying that they did not serve Israeli interests and only delayed the demilitarization of Gaza.

The Israeli military operations in Gaza are taking place as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is campaigning for re-election and portraying himself as key to the country’s security. Jared Kushner, the Trump envoy and son-in-law who has been working with the Board of Peace on plans for Gaza, said earlier this month that Mr. Netanyahu’s government was acting “a little irrational” ahead of the election.

Volker Turk, the United Nations human rights chief, called on Tuesday for international investigators to be allowed into all parts of Gaza to recover the remains of Palestinians still buried under rubble, and to help gather evidence of potential war crimes.

He said in a statement on social media that remains believed to be from 96 people from three Palestinian families were recovered this month, including many women and children. Noting that Palestinian officials have estimated that thousands of people may still be buried under rubble, he said the findings so far “may only be the tip of the iceberg” because “much of Gaza has been flattened by Israeli bombing or demolition and clearing by heavy machinery and explosives.”

Doctors Without Borders said on Sunday said that one of its humanitarian vehicles was damaged and an aid worker injured when an Israeli strike in Gaza City targeted a vehicle less than seven feet away from them. The group said in a post on social media that the aid vehicle was clearly identified and accused Israeli forces of showing “a blatant disregard for the safety of humanitarian and medical personnel.”

“Nowhere is safe in Gaza,” Doctors Without Borders said, calling for civilians, health care workers and other humanitarian staff to be protected.

The Israeli military said in a statement that the attack in Gaza City on Sunday had targeted and killed two Hamas military wing operatives. The Israeli military said that it took steps to mitigate harm to civilians, including using “precise munitions and aerial surveillance.”

The Israeli military’s prosecution of the war in Gaza has come under further scrutiny in the past week after “NAZA,” a documentary about Palestinian civilian deaths in the war, premiered at the Venice International Film Festival. The Israeli directors received a 25-minute standing ovation and won the Special Jury Prize, but faced an official backlash at home.

The Israeli military chief, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, consulted on Monday with top generals about how to respond to the film, saying it was based on “deliberate distortions of reality.”

On Tuesday, at a ceremony marking the start of the Jewish New Year, Maj. Gen. Yaniv Asor, who leads the military’s southern command, insisted on the importance of “maintaining the integrity of our own conduct, distinguishing between the enemy and those who are not involved in the hostilities.” He said this required the military to examine itself and “correct what must be corrected.”

But General Asor also said that Israeli forces would continue to operate in Gaza “to prevent Hamas from rebuilding its capabilities.”

item.title: The A.I. Doomsday Skeptics
item.description:
Remember in early August, when I interviewed Nate Soares, co-author of “If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies”? Back then, writing about the dangers A.I. might pose to humanity’s survival still felt a little niche.

What a difference a month makes. In the last week alone, we’ve heard stories about how A.I. could help build bioweapons or hack into critical infrastructure. Different articles quote different researchers on the odds of A.I. wiping out humanity by the end of the decade. A.I. doomerism has gone mainstream. Or so it seems. Today, my colleague Parin Behrooz writes about the people who don’t think we should be talking about A.I. like this, and what they think we should be doing instead.

By Parin Behrooz

This week, it seemed as if much of the world was struck by the same fear: that A.I. might pose a threat to humanity.

Last week, in the aftermath of a July cyberattack in which A.I. agents self-organized and deceived their human minders, a researcher resigned from Anthropic, claiming neither Anthropic nor OpenAI “is acting responsibly” with this technology. Another senior Anthropic researcher said there was a greater than 10 percent chance A.I. could make humans extinct within a decade. Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, wrote a lengthy essay calling for a slowdown. Other A.I. leaders, including Sam Altman and Elon Musk, agreed. Barack Obama weighed in; King Charles plans to host an A.I. meeting.

The speed of this sudden push for action, and the scope of who’s involved, might give you the impression that a consensus exists — that most people who spend their days thinking about A.I. now agree it threatens the survival of humanity. But my colleague Cade Metz, who has been covering A.I. for more than a decade, told me that isn’t the case.

“When you tell people they’re gonna die, they stand up and listen,” he said. But in reality, “it’s a relatively small group of people who’ve taken over the discourse.”

‘The machine-god narrative’

Those who take issue with the outcry over A.I.’s existential risks are not a united front. Some, including many in the Trump administration, dismiss calls for slowdowns and regulation as a drag on America’s edge in the global A.I. race. (This week, President Trump called A.I. safety concerns “a hoax.”)

Others who work in the industry accuse A.I.’s biggest companies of seeking to stifle competition and tilt the regulatory landscape in their favor. Another group wants stringent regulation, but thinks focusing on A.I. killing us all (rather than, say, taking our jobs) will produce the wrong kind of regulation.

What these skeptics do agree on is that seeing A.I. through the lens of potential doomsday scenarios doesn’t tend to serve the public interest.

I asked Cade to give me some examples of people he thought were good representatives of these perspectives.

He pointed me toward Aidan Gomez, the head of the Canadian A.I. start-up Cohere. Gomez wrote an essay over the weekend, in response to Amodei, with some aggressive criticism. Why, he asked, should a handful of big Silicon Valley companies get to write the safety rules for a generational technology that will be used by the entire world? “Under the pretext of protecting the public,” he wrote, these oligopolies are now trying to dictate the rules of competition.

Gomez does think A.I. needs guardrails. But he wants the process of putting them in place to involve input from many voices, which will necessarily make it slow. Breathless arguments focused on dystopian scenarios serve those who would have us rush.

Cade and I also discussed Timnit Gebru, a prominent A.I. researcher and critic, who left Google in 2020. Gebru calls the current doomsday frenzy a distraction. The real threats, she argues, are already here: A.I. guiding autonomous weapons in active warfare, data centers worsening climate change, and employers using automation as a pretext to cut workers. “This machine-god narrative is, in my opinion, meant to distract us from these,” she told Wired this week.

The computational linguist Emily M. Bender of the University of Washington, who co-wrote the book “The AI Con,” argues that the language used to anthropomorphize A.I. pulls attention away from the people building and deploying it.

The problem with talking so much about dangers like human extinction, these critics argue, is that it takes the energy that could be put toward addressing actual current harms, and redirects it toward hypothetical scenarios.

An old story

Cade recently co-wrote a story aimed at helping people think through this growing fear that A.I. could end humanity. One thing it pointed out is a worldview in Silicon Valley that has always seen the promise of A.I. as inseparable from existential risk. This worldview predates the technology itself. And so when something like the July hacking incident happens, it plays into a pre-existing narrative.

Step outside of that community, Cade told me, and the picture gets more complicated. Many researchers Cade spoke to think autonomous rogue A.I. is unlikely to pose an existential risk for some time, if ever.

The notion that it will is based on the idea that A.I. will keep improving at the rate it has to date. But that’s not a given, Cade said.

“If you talk to serious researchers in this area, even the people who are making these claims,” he said, “they will tell you: We don’t know how to get to that all-powerful point.”

We still don’t know a lot about a technology that has tremendous power both to change the world and to capture the public imagination. At this moment, that may be the most important point of all.

Related: Take a look at how A.I. risks are splitting Silicon Valley and Washington.

Rising fuel prices caused by the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran are setting off protests around the world, especially in the developing countries of Asia.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen accused each other of launching attacks. The Houthis are increasingly using A.I. and other tools to build their own weapons.

The war in Iran has cost the U.S. roughly $38 billion and significantly depleted U.S. munitions.

Denmark’s military said a Russian frigate fired two flares at a Danish air force helicopter.

The U.S. said it had deployed weapons in Earth’s orbit, the first public acknowledgment of American weapons in space.

A U.K. inquiry into the murder of seven babies by Lucy Letby, a neonatal nurse, found systemic failures — but did not consider whether she might not be guilty.

Less than two months before the U.S. midterm elections, Democrats hold a clear advantage over Republicans, according to a new Times/Siena poll.

Paul Sonne, our Moscow bureau chief, traveled to Kyrgyzstan, where the economy grew 11 percent last year, partly because the country has become a key conduit for goods flowing into Russia. Watch the video.

An heir to Thailand’s Singha beer empire has prompted a rare public reckoning over taboo subjects by accusing his brother of sexual abuse.

“Widow’s Bay,” a horror-comedy about a haunted island, won 14 Emmy Awards. You can watch the highlights here.

Prince Harry and Meghan have changed their children’s school because of security concerns.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about a retired archaeologist’s search for the remains of D’Artagnan.

The actress is at the center of a backlash after posing nude behind strategically placed sports gear in advertisements for a betting site. Many female athletes have accused her of encouraging the objectification of women and minimizing their contributions to sports. Creating controversy, though, might be exactly the goal.

Last week, thieves broke into a museum on the French Riviera and made off with two Renoir paintings, the latest in a string of thefts since the Louvre heist last year.

Chinese porcelain, Huguenot crosses, gold and silver coins, Art Nouveau jewelry pieces and a jersey worn by Zinedine Zidane at the World Cup have all have been stolen from museums, large and small, across France. The thefts suggested that the country is struggling to protect its treasures. What’s behind the rise in heists?

Australians love a long road trip into the outback. That’s why it was surprising last month when sales of electric vehicles in the country outstripped sales of gas-powered cars. The transition took some time, with many drivers concerned that electric cars could not handle long road trips.

One major reason for the shift: the Iran war. The closing of the Strait of Hormuz and the fuel shortages that resulted have added another reason for people to strive for energy security. Read more about Australia’s E.V. boom.

Watch: “The Doll” is based on a novel that’s revered in Poland. The Netflix mini-series also has corsets and elaborate wigs.

Brighten: This Ibiza apartment was renovated to feel lighter and more connected to the sea.

Train: Stiffness and soreness from exercise become more noticeable as you get older. Here’s how to adjust your workout.

Appreciate: Yayoi Kusama’s last show before her death opened last week in Amsterdam and includes installations made expressly for the event by the Japanese artist.

These big, creamy butter beans are paired with crisp, broiled broccolini and topped with lemon juice and a bit of chile crisp. They’re always on the menu at Bar Panisse, in Berkeley, Calif., which is on our new list of the 50 best restaurants in the U.S. Check it out.

Here are today’s Spelling Bee, Mini Crossword, Wordle and Sudoku. Find all our games here.

That’s it for today. See you tomorrow! — Katrin

Parin Behrooz was our guest writer today.

We welcome your feedback. Send us your suggestions at theworld@nytimes.com.

item.title: Does the Stork’s Return to Britain Restore History or Rewrite It?
item.description:
The noisy throng of birds beat their wings and hopped up and down in their pen. These 3-month-old white storks, fueled by a generous morning’s feed, were ready for takeoff.

As a keeper twisted open the gate of the pen, a dedicated crowd of bird watchers in stork-themed shirts held its collective breath from several hundred feet away. The sight of a juvenile stork on its first flight is not to be missed.

The lanky bird, fabled in European folklore as a bringer of life, is now a permanent addition to Britain’s skies. It is also a surprisingly contentious one.

To the conservationists behind the yearslong effort to establish a population, the storks’ introduction restores a species that was presumed to have been wiped out in Britain some 600 years ago. To some more skeptical naturalists, it is a misguided act that introduces a bird that had never made Britain its home.

The White Stork Project, as the effort is known, has so far established a colony of some 100 birds at Knepp, a 3,500-acre former dairy farm in West Sussex.

Over two decades, the environment has done most of the reclamation there unaided as part of a wider “rewilding” effort that lets natural processes govern the landscape. But Isabella Tree, the conservationist who co-owns Knepp, is giving it something of a push with the storks.

Unlike other birds that could strike out and breed from just one pair, storks are a sociable species that are more likely to survive in a colony, she said.

To build that colony, conservationists have released captive-bred storks at Knepp every summer for the past eight years. The effort is working: Some 40 nests silhouette the landscape’s oak canopies.

This year’s batch of fledglings was bred at a zoo from flightless birds that had crashed into electrical pylons in Poland. After mingling with the colony’s existing population of wild-hatched chicks, the juveniles are embarking on a thousand-mile seasonal migration to northern Africa this fall. It is a grueling voyage: Most typically die in the attempt, but survivors will return three or four years later to find a mate.

Ms. Tree’s hope is that the colony will eventually become self-sufficient and spread across southern England to form satellite colonies. “We know that we can bring them back,” she said in an interview in July.

As the colony has grown, so has a re-examination of the archaeological and written record of its existence.

Though white storks have been spotted in Britain over the centuries, some researchers say there is little sign they made more than fleeting visits.

“We have no evidence from any source whatsoever that there were ever areas in Britain with a significant stork population,” said Ulrich Schmölcke, an archaeologist who specializes in birds at the Leibniz Center for Archaeology in Mainz, Germany.

By that logic, Knepp might be Britain’s first white stork colony ever.

The question has opened a ferocious debate over how actively conservationists should reshape the wilderness.

Archaeologists have unearthed the occasional adult white stork bone in Britain, but they have never found juvenile remains that would show the birds were not just visitors, Dr. Schmölcke said.

Nor do white storks appear in Britain’s rich canon of folk tales or written laws, he pointed out, as they do in parts of Europe where they are unquestionably native breeders.

The evidence, Dr. Schmölcke said, suggested “they never established a stable population.”

Ian Carter, an ornithologist who previously worked with the official environmental body Natural England, objected to the managed release of white storks on that basis. “No matter how many times people say it’s a ‘reintroduction,’ it absolutely isn’t,” he said.

The birds could pose a threat to existing wildlife, because they breed in high densities and prey on vulnerable wetland creatures, Mr. Carter said. “You can’t impose a species on the environment without having knock-on effects on other species,” he added. “And it changes the meaning of wildlife if you can just pick and choose any bird.”

The uproar prompted Natural England to weigh in with an assessment. In May, it said it had determined that white storks were never a native breeding bird.

Although the birds had visited from continental Europe, researchers could locate only a single historical reference to a nesting pair: In 1416, a Scottish priest observed two white storks building a nest on the roof of St Giles’ Cathedral in Edinburgh before they flew off. It was not clear from the text whether they bred successfully.

“It’s an animal that has turned up here sporadically,” said Tony Juniper, the chairman of Natural England. “But we can’t convince ourselves yet that this was an established species.”

While Mr. Juniper was effusive about the broader effort to “rewild” Knepp with native plants and other animals, he said the environmental authorities could not actively support the introduction of a species without an established breeding history in Britain.

In response to the skeptics, Ms. Tree said the standard of evidence they demanded — juvenile remains or legal records mentioning breeding — was impossibly high.

Storks were part of medieval Britain, she said, pointing to their appearance in artworks and place names. One is Storrington, a village near Knepp.

“Ultimately, you can argue either way,” Ms. Tree said. “And I don’t think it matters.”

The birds’ prominence as a symbol of fertility persists in cartoons and old-fashioned euphemisms about childbirth. A common theory for the link traces it to migration patterns: Storks would return to the skies of medieval Europe in February and March, coinciding with increases in human births around nine months after midsummer weddings.

Germanic mythology held that storks delivered the souls of newborn babies from subterranean lakes, said Ms. Tree, who is writing a book on the birds. In the early 19th century, the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen adapted that idea in “The Storks,” a short story with a depiction of long-legged birds delivering newborns.

Bringing the birds to England has justifications beyond historical rectitude, Ms. Tree said. The storks’ large nests provide homes and food for other birds, she said. And the storks benefit from access to a cooler climate as continental Europe warms.

“We need to allow species to be able to move north in response to climate change,” she said.

While Ms. Tree’s critics contest her rationale, their objections are not a serious obstacle to her work. The releases at Knepp are independently funded and do not require official permission.

Mr. Juniper and Dr. Schmölcke both said that storks from mainland Europe could push north into Britain as the climate changes, regardless of the effort at Knepp.

At the estate in July, debates over their presence did not seem to concern the young storks as they took flight. Humans may have started the colony, but the birds did what feathered creatures tend to do. One by one they emerged from the pen, outstretched their wings and, after a few false starts, took flight.

Days later, the birds had embarked on their migration across the English Channel. Within weeks, some had been spotted in Morocco, scavenging in a garbage dump.

Jamie Craig, the zookeeper who had opened the pen to free the birds, responded with a resigned laugh to the image of them feasting on trash. “That’s life, that’s nature,” he said. “If we give it a resource, it will use it.”

item.title: The World Economy Is Becoming Wary of the U.S.
item.description:
Global investors are balking at U.S. bonds. Talk of the dollar’s dwindling power is getting louder. Foreign governments are hauling their gold out of American vaults.

Almost two years into President Trump’s second term, the world economy is increasingly looking for ways to distance itself from America. Concerns about a $40 trillion debt burden, the excessive use of sanctions to solve foreign policy problems and Mr. Trump’s penchant for pushing the limits of the rule of law are raising questions about the appeal of the United States as a haven for global investment.

Despite pledges by foreign companies and nations to invest in the United States — in many cases to curry favor with the White House — capital is starting to seek alternative destinations.

“Geopolitical factors and U.S. weaponization of the dollar through financial sanctions are causing central banks and other official investors to attempt to diversify away from dollar assets,” said Eswar Prasad, the former head of the International Monetary Fund’s China division.

The United States is not yet an investment pariah. Private investors are still pouring money into American financial markets and stocks, artificial intelligence infrastructure is booming and no rival currency is poised to topple the dollar imminently.

In testimony before Congress on Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that he remained confident in the credibility of the U.S. financial system, arguing that bond auctions continue to operate successfully and that the dollar is still thriving as measured by its share of global transactions.

“The U.S. is in fact the leader, and the leader does not fear competition,” Mr. Bessent said. “Competition makes us better.”

But cracks in America’s economic dominance are starting to show.

The most glaring example has been in the bond market. Yields have been soaring as investors nervous about the mounting national debt demand a higher rate of return for buying Treasury bonds. This week, the yield on the 10-year Treasury topped 5 percent, reaching its highest level since 2007.

A decision to raise rates on Wednesday could help to alleviate concerns about the Fed’s grip on elevated inflation, fears that have injected more jitters into bond markets.

The ominous bond threshold was crossed a week after the Treasury Department purchased $5.2 billion of its own debt maturing in the next 10 to 20 years, part of a plan to inject demand into the Treasury market to try to push prices higher and yields lower. Mr. Bessent said investors were failing to understand the underlying strength of the economy and dared them to bet against him.

“It’s my dream,” Mr. Bessent said last week at Southern Methodist University. “I have asymmetric information. I am the house now.”

With the United States’ long-term fiscal situation looking shaky, some countries are starting to wonder if America is a wise investment. This month, Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, the largest in the world, said it planned to reduce its holdings of U.S. Treasuries as it looks elsewhere for stronger returns.

And then there is the future of the dollar.

Nearly 90 percent of global foreign exchange transactions are in dollars. But the share of dollars being held in central bank reserves has been steadily declining over the past decade, falling to 56 percent at the end of 2025 from 64 percent in 2015.

Last year, Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, said erratic policymaking in the United States was setting the stage for a “global euro moment.”

The United States has taken advantage of the greenback’s special status to use it as a foreign policy tool, imposing stiff sanctions on adversaries such as Iran and Russia. As the United States ramps up its use of sanctions to resolve global conflicts, the permanence of the dollar as the world’s reserve currency has come into question with greater frequency.

This year, the United States tried to start scaling back its sanctions program amid worries that an overuse of financial warfare was leading other countries to seek alternatives to the dollar. The dollar is used in most cross-border financial transactions, so sanctions can essentially cut off a country’s ability to interact with the Western financial system. Frustrated with how the United States uses its economic might, more countries are seeking alternative financial systems that America cannot touch.

However, Mr. Bessent reversed course in August when he announced Operation Economic Outcast. The initiative aims to strangle Iran’s economy and threatens secondary sanctions on any country that maintains economic ties to Tehran. Even the Treasury secretary acknowledged that if the United States is forced to make good on that threat, it could “blow up the global financial system.”

Although the euro and China’s renminbi do not appear ready to overtake the dollar anytime soon, the emergence of central bank digital currencies, stablecoins and cryptocurrencies give U.S. adversaries new avenues to circumvent the American financial system when making international transactions.

China has been leading the development of a cross-border digital currency platform with Hong Kong, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia that would allow money to move more quickly and with lower fees than what is possible with traditional banking transactions. A similar cross-border payments project led by some Group of 7 nations and Western financial institutions is also in development but is not as far along as China’s initiative, which is known as mBridge.

Russia and India said last week that they are working on a plan that would let them use central bank digital currencies to settle international trade payments. Such a mechanism would allow the countries to expand their trade relationship and reduce reliance on Western financial institutions that can be targeted by U.S. sanctions.

“The story of moving away from the dollar is one of the oldest stories that exists,” said Josh Lipsky, the chair of international economics at the Atlantic Council. “Countries have thought about working around the dollar, and technology is making it a little cheaper and easier to do it than before.”

While some countries are focused on digital money, others are going for the gold as they fret about the stability of the United States.

In 2025, world international reserves held in gold surpassed foreign official holdings of U.S. Treasury securities. This year, the price of gold exceeded $5,000 per troy ounce for the first time in history as central banks stocked up on the metal amid intensifying global conflicts and concerns over inflation.

Demand for gold is so high that some countries also want to keep theirs closer to home. With geopolitical unrest rising and Mr. Trump lobbing tariff threats against European allies, some have even taken the rare step of relocating the gold that they keep in vaults at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

This month, the central bank of the Netherlands said it transferred a large part of its 95 tons of North American gold reserves out of the United States, citing “increasing geopolitical unrest” and the need to be prepared for crisis. In March, the Bank of France said it pulled 129 tons of gold from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and moved it to Paris.

The Trump administration has not threatened to seize foreign gold held in the United States, but Mr. Trump has raised questions about his views of international law by floating the idea of colonizing places like Greenland and Canada.

“It’s like the countries don’t trust the U.S.,” said Daniel Tannebaum, who served as the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control compliance coordinator for the New York Fed. “I do think that there is a fear factor.”

That fear factor is also creating blowback for American companies that are trying to do business abroad.

Mr. Tannebaum, who is a partner in Oliver Wyman’s risk and public policy practice, said that the aggressive use of tariffs and export controls by the United States has made European countries and companies wary of adopting American technology for sensitive industries such as artificial intelligence. They worry that if they are dependent on the United States for such infrastructure it could be used against them if Washington decides to ban or disable the technology, as it has done during disputes with China and Russia.

All of this has contributed to an erosion of America’s status as a safe haven.

“Governments and companies now have to ask what would happen if the United States turned its economic leverage against them,” Mr. Tannebaum said.

item.title: Japan Reaches a Unique Milestone, With More Than 100,000 People Aged 100 or Over
item.description:
There are now more than 100,000 centenarians in Japan, a record for a country famous for its longevity.

Japan’s health ministry released data on Tuesday showing that there are now 107,677 people who are at least 100 years old, an increase of nearly 8,000 since last year. The oldest woman, Fuyo Kishimoto from Kyoto, is 114 and the oldest man, Hikaru Kato from Kumamoto, is 112. Women make up the vast majority of the group, at 88 percent.

Japan’s health minister, Kenichiro Ueno, welcomed the news on Tuesday, and pledged to build a strong social security system that supports the elderly in living long and healthy lives. “I am very happy that so many people have been able to stay active for so long,” he said at a news conference in Tokyo.

Stuart Gietel-Basten, a professor of social science at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, said the long lives of many Japanese could be attributed to healthy diet, active daily routines, and an affordable health system with regular check ups.

Women are overrepresented as centenarians because many men of that generation died in World War II, and those who survived smoked and drank more than women, he said. Men are also more likely to be involved in industrial work, which could have long-term health impacts. Many men became isolated after retirement or the loss of a spouse, he added, and women tended to be more engaged in their communities, which improved their mental health.

Tetsuo Sato, 106, is one of the 100,000, living in the rice-growing village of Osonogo in the mountainous Niigata Prefecture with his son, daughter-in-law, dog and cat.

Hard of hearing and visually impaired, Mr. Sato fills his days by making notebooks from old calendars and wrapping paper. He also tells stories about his experiences fighting in the Battle of Imphal during World War II.

His daughter-in-law, Kuniko Sato, 68, said he was determined to be self-sufficient and continued to bathe himself without help.

“When I injured my leg last year, Grandpa started washing his own rice bowls,” she said. “We ended up caring for each other in our old age.”

As well as a rapidly aging population, Japan is grappling with one of the lowest birthrates in the world, a predicament that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called a “quiet emergency.”

Japan’s population peaked at 128 million in 2008, and is projected to drop to 87 million by 2070, according to government projections. The country now has roughly the same number of people as it did in 1989. For every new birth in the country, there are two deaths.

The demographic crisis poses challenges for the government, as it drives up the tax burden on a shrinking work force. For decades, the Japanese authorities have tried to rebalance the rapidly aging population by encouraging couples to have more children, to little avail.

Some experts argue that Japan needs to allow more immigrants to offset the population decline. But a wave of nationalist sentiment has recently swept the country, with some activists calling for even stricter controls as part of a “Japan First” movement.

At the same time, the country’s centenarians are determined to remain active. Some are even still working.

In two days, Mr. Sato will turn 107. More than a dozen members of his family plan to celebrate at a traditional hot spring hotel, where they hope to photograph the four generations gathered together.

Ms. Sato said her father-in-law “seems to feel a sense of responsibility, believing that a parent must always look out for their children, he likely feels he needs to stay strong and capable.”

“His original goal was to live to 100, but now he aims to reach 110,” she added.

item.title: A Corruption Case Spawns Memes and Indignation Among Ukrainians
item.description:
Ukrainians are used to revelations of corruption in their government. But one case that emerged this month has managed to grab their attention, in part because of a vivid turn of phrase.

An official working under Ukraine’s top prosecutor was caught on tape by anticorruption investigators describing his own approach to enriching himself through corruption.

“If you’re going to do something, then go all in — boom,” the official was recorded saying. He then explained, profanely, what he meant. If you’re going to sleep with a woman, he said, then sleep with “a queen.” And if you’re going to steal, then steal “a million.”

According to investigators, the official, Serhiy Kropyva, and others in the Office of the Prosecutor General did just that — the stealing part, anyway — through kickbacks they received for covering up a network of phone scammers working in Ukraine and abroad.

The allegations toppled the prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, who was formally removed from office on Tuesday by Parliament after President Volodymyr Zelensky called for his ouster. Mr. Kravchenko had already resigned last week.

He denies wrongdoing. He left Ukraine in recent days, saying that he was traveling abroad to discuss the work of anti-corruption bodies in Ukraine with partner countries — an explanation greeted with eye-rolls by his countrymen.

The official on the tape, Mr. Kropyva, has been arrested and is in pretrial detention. He at first denied that it was his voice but has since backed away from that claim. He says he is innocent of corruption.

The colorful recording has spawned memes as well as bitterness among Ukrainians. They have been sacrificing for their homeland, including through regular donations to the army, only to see an endless parade of officials accused of illicitly filling their own pockets.

Many Ukrainians see graft as a threat not only to the war effort but also to the country’s future. At the same time, they voice pride in the justice meted out in such cases, seeing it as a sign that the country’s democracy, including independent anti-corruption agencies, remains healthy after nearly five years of all-out war.

The scandal involving the Office of the Prosecutor General comes at a delicate moment for Mr. Zelensky, who has come under pressure to clean house amid the drip-drip-drip of corruption cases.

The revelations are especially stinging at a time when Ukraine is badly lacking money for the war. They threaten to sow doubts among the country’s European partners just as Ukraine asks for help in plugging its yawning budget gaps.

Russia has escalated attacks on the Ukrainian economy, striking warehouses, gas stations, railways and energy infrastructure with jet-powered drones for which Ukraine has not yet found an effective defense. The country’s prime minister, Serhii Koretskyi, said last week that Russian assaults would deprive the state of about $1.5 billion.

A clash over Ukraine’s anti-corruption efforts came to a head last year, when people took to the streets to safeguard the autonomy of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine, known as NABU, and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office. Both were created a decade ago with strong Western backing.

The Zelensky administration had moved to curb their power by placing them under the authority of the prosecutor general, who is approved by Parliament, where the president’s party holds a majority. Mr. Zelensky reversed course in the face of the demonstrations.

The prosecutor general who would have overseen the anti-corruption agencies was Mr. Kravchenko, the man who has now been felled in a corruption case.

Since the 2025 protests that preserved its independence, NABU has accused dozens of officials of corruption. The most highly publicized case, involving graft in the energy sector, led to the dismissal of Andriy Yermak, the powerful head of Mr. Zelensky’s office.

According to a survey conducted this summer by the Center for Social and Marketing Research in Kyiv, a majority of Ukrainians see corruption as having a stronger impact on the country than Russian bombings.

“These corruption scandals are terrible, and they are certainly demoralizing,” said Dmytro Kalach, 38, who works in light manufacturing and regularly donates money to the army.

He said that the graft would not deter him from continuing to support the military.

“The fact that they are scoundrels,” he said of government officials accused of corruption, “doesn’t mean I have to be a scoundrel like them.”

Some Ukrainians said they would carry on doing whatever it took to survive despite the corruption but still felt deeply hurt when cases came to light.

“I cannot simply shrug off these corruption scandals,” said Viacheslav Oksiuta, 68, a retiree from the military. He continues to work in the defense sector and is the father of two sons, one of whom is serving in the army.

“I can’t even watch television when I hear about these cases,” he said. “I take all of this very personally.”

Even as Parliament was taking action against Mr. Kravchenko this week, the drumbeat of corruption accusations carried on. Investigators said on Tuesday that they had discovered another illegal enrichment scheme, this time in a tax service office in western Ukraine.

item.title: Kosovo’s Former Leader Is Sentenced to 25 Years in War Crimes Case
item.description:
Hashim Thaci, the former leader of Kosovo who led its bloody independence fight against Serbia in the 1990s, was sentenced on Wednesday to 25 years in prison for war crimes, including arbitrary detention, torture and murder.

Mr. Thaci’s sentence concluded a trial that has deepened divisions in his Balkan homeland over whether he should be feted as a war hero or condemned as a leader of violent rebels.

Mr. Thaci, 58, who has long denied wrongdoing, was sentenced along with three other senior members of the since-disbanded Kosovo Liberation Army, or K.L.A. A special tribunal in The Hague, known as the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, handed down the judgments.

During the conflict in the 1990s, the four men “contributed significantly” to the targeting of perceived opponents, the tribunal said in a statement. Some of the victims were fellow Kosovo Albanians perceived as collaborators or traitors. Others were members of ethnic minorities, the tribunal said.

“The targeting of such opponents took the form of killings; arrests and detention without due process; physical and psychological mistreatment; as well as other forms of abuse, intimidation and harassment,” the tribunal said.

In most cases, the tribunal found no evidence that the men’s victims “had engaged in any criminal activity, taken an active part in hostilities or presented any other legitimate security concern” for the K.L.A.

“The vast majority of them were innocent civilians,” the tribunal said.

For years, the case has divided Kosovo, a tiny country that has long been one of the poorest parts of the former Yugoslavia.

Mr. Thaci, long a towering figure in Kosovo, has led the country as both its prime minister and its president. In June 2020, when he was still serving as president, the news of his indictment took him by surprise: He was in Vienna, on his way to the White House for peace talks with Serbia.

That November, he resigned and surrendered to the tribunal in The Hague. He was in detention there through the trial, which started in 2023.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

item.title: At Least 16 Dead in Gaza After Building Collapse, Officials Say
item.description:
A war-damaged building in Gaza collapsed on Wednesday, killing at least 16 people and trapping many more beneath the wreckage, according to Gaza’s Civil Defense rescue service.

Dozens were living in the complex, the Saada residential building in Gaza City, when it caved in at around 2 a.m. local time, officials from the service said. Civil Defense is a part of the Hamas-run interior ministry in Gaza.

The officials added that the building had previously been hit by an Israeli strike, though it was unclear when. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Search-and-rescue teams pulled survivors from the wreckage on Wednesday morning as they searched for missing residents.

“We can see people still trapped under the rubble,” said Raed al-Dahshan, director of Civil Defense in the Gaza City area, who is involved in the rescue efforts. “We’re doing everything we can to extract them.”

He said that the authorities in Gaza had warned residents that the building was unstable, but that many did not leave because they did not want to be displaced and potentially end up in worse conditions. Mr. al-Dahshan said that there were roughly 70 buildings in the Gaza City area at risk of collapse.

The deadly collapse underscores the devastation across Gaza, where years of punishing conflict between Israel and Hamas have left entire neighborhoods in ruins. Much of Gaza’s population was displaced by the conflict, and many are now living in damaged buildings.

After a U.S.-brokered cease-fire was agreed in October 2025, Palestinians had hoped that Israel would allow a significant amount of heavy machinery and construction materials into Gaza to begin the long process of removing rubble and rebuilding. Thousands of bodies remain missing beneath the rubble across Gaza from years of war, according to local officials.

Efforts by President Trump’s Board of Peace and regional mediators to advance the cease-fire and pave the way for reconstruction have stalled. Israel has continued to strike the territory, despite international pressure to halt its attacks there.

On Tuesday, an Israeli strike killed a Civil Defense worker and a teenager, according to an official in the rescue service. The Israeli military said it had been targeting Hamas militants, and that the attack was under review.

The International Committee of the Red Cross and Egyptian-backed rescue teams assisted local emergency crews on Wednesday in their search for survivors of the building collapse.

In a statement, Ramiz Alakbarov, the United Nations humanitarian coordinator for the occupied Palestinian territory, urged international authorities to allow heavy equipment into Gaza to assist in search-and-rescue operations, along with vital humanitarian aid.

“Every possible effort must be made to save lives, protect people from further harm and provide families with safer places to live,” he said. “Every minute counts.”

item.title: Rising Fuel Prices Set Off Anger and Protests Around the World
item.description:
The world is furious — again — over rising energy prices caused by the American-Israeli war against Iran.

Since the latest surge pushed oil above $100 a barrel, protesters have burned tires and cars in Guatemala and Syria to express their rage.

Portugal’s roads have featured cars crawling in protest with honking horns after diesel reached a record high of more than $9 a gallon.

And especially in the developing countries of Asia, which are heavily reliant on Middle Eastern energy and deep in debt from earlier efforts to offset the war’s impacts, transport systems and governments are facing another round of enormous strain.

Fuel shortages and long lines at the pump are slowing economies along with strikes by taxi drivers and laborers who see no point in working when earnings barely cover energy costs.

Many countries are confronting a difficult question: Is it riskier to pass on price increases to a combustible public, accelerating inflation, or bolster subsidies and aid that would drive up public debt and possibly threaten the stability of national currencies?

“How much fiscal capacity does Asia or the developing world have in general to manage this geopolitical crisis?” said Sana Jaffrey, a lecturer at the Australian National University who researches conflict and state-building in Asia. “What happens to global financial markets when that capacity starts to run out?”

“At some point,” she added, “it’s going to become everyone’s problem.”

Here are some global flash points The New York Times is monitoring.

In Makassar, South Sulawesi, residents this week reported shortages of cooking gas, rolling blackouts and a sudden move toward gasoline rationing.

Across the provincial capital, drivers pushed motorbikes with empty tanks or left them in long lines near pumps with nothing to give. Taxi drivers held a protest on Monday against a new rationing system organized by odd and even license plate numbers.

Tensions have also been rising in Yogyakarta, in Java. Students demonstrated against surging fuel prices on Monday — only to have their rally broken up by aggressive pro-government organizations.

Discussions about ending subsidized fuel access for wealthy and middle-class households have been intensifying. The government’s calculations before the war assumed oil prices would be at around $70 a barrel, and public debt has soared since the conflict started.

Fishermen along Manila Bay who use boats powered by diesel or gas had hoped this week to venture out to sea after weeks of monsoon rains. Large numbers are now staying in port.

“Many were raring to go back to fish, but have no money to buy gas,” said Fernando Hicap, the national chairman of a major fishing association. “The new round of price adjustments have been choking many of us to death.”

Bus and ride-share drivers have also been marching in Quezon City, and quietly protesting by not working — a trend also popping up elsewhere. In Vietnam over the weekend, drivers with Grab, a ride-hailing app, called for a boycott to protest low pay caused in part by rising fuel costs.

Modesto Floranda, the leader of a 70,000-strong group of Filipino bus drivers and owners, said that working 15 to 18 hours a day now only earns enough for a single meal.

The government has offered one-time payments of about $80 to public transportation drivers.

“It is not enough,” he said.

Transport workers and Indigenous activists marched through the streets of Guatemala City recently, demanding more than stopgap measures like price caps and subsidies.

Some groups have called for a suspension of fuel taxes and a shift away from fossil fuels, which critics see as a source for elite enrichment and environmental damage. Farmers across Latin America, heavily reliant on diesel for tractors, have been especially frustrated.

At one recent march in Guatemala, where videos showed a thick throng of workers, an organizer with a megaphone characterized the economic struggle as a contest between governments and the wealthy, and everyone else.

“They are in a place of luxury, that’s why they don’t think about our misery, hunger, or the cost of the basic food needs of the working class,” he said. “We will also continue to put pressure on them.”

A few days later, in Villa Nueva, just south of the capital, videos showed cars set ablaze in the streets.

Organizing mainly on social media, Portuguese drivers gathered last week for several “buzinões” — protests with cars driving slowly while honking. They caused traffic jams across several key thoroughfares including the 25 de Abril Bridge in Lisbon.

In a sign of growing frustration with large oil and gas interests, one vehicle convoy blocked access to roads near a major refinery in Sines, according to a local news site.

Naomi Hossain, a political sociologist at the University of London who has studied the impacts of energy shocks, said that it was common for people to assume that fossil fuel costs and inflation rise “because of collusion between political elites and businesses.”

“There are good reasons to believe that untamed inflation is pushing voters to the right,” she said. “Centrist governments don’t seem to be able to do much to protect people against these shocks, and there are no realistic left alternatives in most places. So one consequence is it’s feeding populism.”

Bangladesh imports more than 90 percent of the petroleum it uses, and most of it comes from the Middle East.

Shortages in the liquid natural gas needed to produce electricity have led to rationing and the temporary closure of garment factories — the main engine of the country’s economy. Many turned to diesel after the war in Iran started in February, only to see those prices now rising.

Robiul Hasan Mehedi, an officer at a garment factory in Bangladesh’s garment hub, Gazipur, said Tuesday that power cuts are now happening four or five times a day.

Several hours of work stoppage — multiplied by dozens of factories and thousands of workers — is now the norm.

Nahid Islam, an opposition leader, said in a protest rally in Dhaka this month that the crowds were marching in part “against those who are forming syndicates around gas, oil and electricity and trying to increase prices.”

Sri Lanka’s government sets fuel prices each month, but fuel distributors that sell to gas stations have started restricting supply as they wait for an expected surge.

“They’re operating at a loss,” Kumara Rajapaksha, the chair of the Filling Station Owners’ Association, told reporters on Monday.

Anura Karunathilaka, Sri Lanka’s energy minister, said that officials were considering whether to raise official prices and add subsidies. The country’s debt to gross domestic product ratio is already among the highest in the developing world.

Just a few hours after the government said that it would temporarily raise prices for gasoline, diesel and other petroleum products by as much as 40 percent, Syrians took to the streets.

Angry crowds in several cities gathered in squares, blocked traffic, and set tires on fire, calling for the price surge to be canceled.

In one video posted online, a man poured what he said was gasoline over his head and threatened to set himself on fire before a crowd intervened.

Government officials said that they had no choice but to raise prices because of the war.

Reporting was contributed by Tiago Carrasco in Lisbon; Rin Hindryati in Bogor, Indonesia; Jason Gutierrez in Manila; Saif Hasnat in Dhaka, Bangladesh; Pamodi Waravita in Colombo, Sri Lanka; Raja Abdulrahim in Amman, Jordan; Hari Kumar in New Delhi; and Tung Ngo in Hanoi, Vietnam.

item.title: Can an Island Nation’s Rugby Dreams Change Its Fortunes?
item.description:
Before the game, the children clear what they can of the dirt field in the heart of Port Moresby, the capital of Papua New Guinea. They pick up soda bottle caps, scraps of trash and jagged gravel from between clumps of dead grass.

The players may be small — pants sliding off, jerseys down to their knees, shoelaces straining to hold up too-large boots — but the stakes feel anything but. These are the semifinals, a make-or-break moment for the Taurama Funky Sharks 10-and-under team, taking on the Junior Nomads.

The team’s 29-year-old coach, Gogobe Simi, gives a pep talk about it being “now or never.” The players scurry onto the field, the bullhorn sounds, and the game is on. Written in crude marker on the taped hands of a team waiting to play is a Bible verse, Philippians 4:13. “I can do all things.”

“For us, it’s really serious,” says Samuel David, 17, who is supporting the Sharks.

Rugby league, it is often said, is akin to a religion in Papua New Guinea.

Gold miners from Australia brought the sport — a faster, more aggressive iteration of rugby that split off from the more widely played rugby union in the 1890s — to Papua New Guinea in the 1930s. It has since become a national obsession, a universal pastime and a force for unity in a fragmented place of more than 800 languages and even more tribal groups.

The sport has such an ardent following in Papua New Guinea that Australia is attempting to cement its influence over the country through the game. It has committed to spending 600 million Australian dollars — about $430 million — to give Papua New Guinea its own team in the sport’s premier professional competition, the National Rugby League of Australia.

The deal is not without conditions: Australian officials have described a clause in the agreement that allows for the funding to be pulled and the team to be scrapped should Papua New Guinea enter into a security pact with China.

It’s a soft-power play by Australia over an island nation less than 100 miles to its north that played a vital strategic role in World War II. In recent years, China has invested in infrastructure projects, offered policing assistance and built a gleaming new school. When the rugby league deal was put forward, Papua New Guinea was “within days” of entering into a policing agreement with China, according to an Australian official who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss matters of intelligence.

It is easy to see why Australia chose rugby league as a vehicle to counter China’s influence.

Gleeful children play the sport for hours on end, barefoot on a dusty stretch of road glistening with specks of glass. They play with plastic bottles stuffed with grass instead of a ball, with rice bags stuffed with newspaper. Rugby jerseys hang in market stalls and from clotheslines, and any television playing a game attracts a rowdy crowd that despairs whenever a power outage renders the screen blank.

“If you’re a politician in P.N.G., you won’t imperil this deal,” the Australian official said. “It would be akin to the mayor of New York doing something to kill the Yankees off.”

Fiona Lahui, mother of the Funky Sharks’ fullback Isaac, put it more simply: “Papua New Guinea has a heart of rugby.”

The aspirations of countless young Papua New Guineans playing the sport — and it is a young nation, with a third of its population under the age of 15 — grew in scale with the news that the Papua New Guinea Chiefs are set to make their debut in the Australian league in 2028.

The Chiefs’ roster will be filled with established athletes playing in Australia and some who have come up through Papua New Guinea’s junior leagues, with players up to 19 years old.

“We play for our community, represent our country, then, N.R.L.,” said Alex Endie, 21, who plays on the Southern Sons, a team of young men from 2 Mile, one of Port Moresby’s urban settlements where people live in largely informal dwellings.

The Chiefs’ entry into Australia’s professional league may be too late for Mr. Endie’s cohort, but younger boys in the community will dream bigger for it, said his friend and teammate, Andrew Lohia, 19.

“The small ones, their aim is to be P.N.G. Chiefs in the future,” Mr. Lohia said from the sidelines of an under-17s game, as Mr. Endie shouted to the field, “Play wide, play wide!”

Chiefs players will earn six-figure salaries, a world away from the daily economic realities of most people in Papua New Guinea, which has a gross domestic product per capita of about $3,000 and where 40 percent of residents live in poverty.

Mr. Endie hasn’t been able to finish his studies to become a machinist because his father lost his job and the family can no longer afford his school fees. He and Mr. Lohia instead spend most their days doing what residents call “marketing” — selling grilled sausages and betel nut, a seed chewed as a mild stimulant (each for about 25 cents); and fatty cuts of lamb (for around $1.50) on the roadside.

The country’s prime minister, James Marape, has referred to the National Rugby League team as a “national unity strategy” that can ameliorate ethnic tensions and address the issue of tribal violence. He compared the team’s introduction to South Africa’s post-apartheid victory in the 1995 rugby union World Cup, which brought white and Black fans together.

The opposition has criticized the investment in a sports team over basic infrastructure needs — passable roads, reliable access to water or health care — as a “bread-and-circuses” approach.

“I would have preferred the government spend money on education and health,” said Juliet Amos, whose two sons play with the Funky Sharks. Even so, she said she appreciated the sport’s positive influence on young people with few opportunities who might otherwise resort to petty crime or gang violence.

“Better to have kids here than out there, trying to do stuff like breaking laws,” she said.

Well before Australia’s overtures, rugby league had been shaping lives in Papua New Guinea.

Angelica Nanege, 30, started playing casual games with other girls as a teenager in the Highlands region deep in the country’s interior. At the time, boys and men would relentlessly mock and heckle them for daring to play.

“Go stay at home, cook for your mama,” they would yell, throwing sticks, stones and water bottles, abuse that lasted for years, she recalled. The girls kept playing and the attitudes toward them slowly changed.

“Now they’re watching and supporting us,” said Ms. Nanege, who has represented Papua New Guinea as a member of the women’s national team, the Papua New Guinea Orchids, and currently plays for the semiprofessional Mount Hagen Eagles.

“We’re not just housewives, we can do anything, just like men,” she said.

On a recent Wednesday morning, at a tin shed gym next to a sweet potato field on the outskirts of Mount Hagen, Ms. Nanege was nursing an injured shoulder from the previous weekend’s game. Her teammates ran through circuits on rusted barbells, holding a plank while singing a children’s song in Tok Pisin.

Part of Australia’s investment is going to an academy program that aims to to bridge the gap in opportunities and training with players in Australia and identify and cultivate a generation of homegrown talent of young Papua New Guineans who may eventually fill the ranks of the Chiefs.

Joey Grima, an Australian coach who has been building the pathways program for Papua New Guinea youth for three years, said that even though just a few of the hundreds of boys and girls in the academy will make it to the big leagues, they will nonetheless learn discipline and life skills that will lead to other opportunities.

He speaks proudly of 18 players who last year went back to school after having quit education so that they could participate in the program, which requires academic enrollment. Papua New Guinea has some of the lowest student retention rates in the region.

Stanley Olo, a former professional player who founded the grass roots league for settlement children that the Funky Sharks play in, said the rough pockets of Port Moresby were home to children brimming with raw talent who could come to dominate the sport.

“We have speed, we have strength, we have everything but discipline and skill,” he said.

“P.N.G. people are a natural fit to be rugby players,” says Arnold Krewanty, who played for the men’s national team, the Papua New Guinea Kumuls, and played in the N.R.L. in 1989. “People here are warriors.”

All that is evident on the overcast Sunday morning when the Funky Sharks are battling the Nomads. Most certainly in the eyes of Mr. Simi, the coach, who trails them around the field like an anxious parent, feverishly protesting a referee’s call that favors the opponents.

“They’re small in size but big in brain,” says the coach, who is not much taller than his charges. “Someday, they’re going to grow up and play in the Chiefs.”

On this day, though, their run ends with an 8-6 loss. Tears are shed, snot is wiped away, yellow and black jerseys are sloughed off.

With mothers, brothers and sisters, they trudge up the street to take two buses back to their settlement in Taurama. There, by late afternoon, with a birthday party in full swing, they will be back to playing rugby.

item.title: Migrants Fear Discrimination After Far Right Surge in German State
item.description:
After polls closed in a German state election this month, dozens of local pro-migrant activists gathered anxiously for dinner to see how big a win the anti-immigrant far right would secure.

When exit polls flashed onscreen showing a wide lead for the Alternative for Germany, an anti-immigrant party, the activists fell quiet, several said in interviews. When the party’s landslide victory was confirmed, guests left early, some in tears.

“After the result, no one felt like eating anymore,” said Amidou Traore, 57, a social worker originally from Ivory Coast who attended the gathering and described experiencing rising hostility to foreigners in the buildup to the election. “When you see this kind of thing, you feel despair.”

Across the state of Saxony-Anhalt, immigrants and their supporters are bracing for the possibility that the Alternative for Germany, widely known by its German initials AfD, could form a coalition to govern the state in the coming weeks. Though it fell short of an outright majority in the statehouse, the AfD can enter office if it wins the support of a small populist party — a move that would give power to the far right for the first time in any German state since 1945.

The AfD campaigned on conducting mass deportations of refugees, replacing foreign workers with Germans, refocusing education on German nationalism and ethnic pride, and pulling state funding for government centers and nonprofit organizations that support immigrants.

AfD leaders doubled down on some of those pledges after the election, even though state governments lack the authority to enact some of the proposals. Ulrich Siegmund, the party’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, said last week that he was willing to use military equipment to carry out deportations.

Now, refugees and foreign workers are considering leaving for other German states or abroad. International students are hoping that their universities make good on promises to shield them from any government backlash. Migrant rights activists say they are strategizing about how to protect vulnerable people in this new era, while aid organizations are searching for new donors.

In Magdeburg, the state capital, we interviewed 16 immigrants, some of whom had lived in Germany for decades, others for just a few years. Many had obtained citizenship or permanent residency, while others had pending asylum claims or lacked legal status.

Most described experiencing rising hostility and discrimination on the streets during the election period, and expressed deep fear and uncertainty about what lay ahead.

Afsaneh Mehrpouyan, 33, an Iranian immunologist, moved to northern Germany in 2022 to conduct medical research, then transferred a year ago to a university in Magdeburg. Now, she said, she and her family are considering relocating again because they fear the AfD will make it harder for immigrants to live in the state.

“For those of us that are working here legally, we specialize in a field and we’re helping this country,” she said, alluding to how foreign workers fill gaps in key sectors like health care. Now, she wonders “if we’ll be treated second-class or if we will be treated equally.”

The AfD’s opposition to immigration has driven its popularity in Saxony-Anhalt, as well as across Germany, particularly since the country accepted 890,000 refugees in 2015, at the peak of Europe’s migration crisis.

Though migration to Saxony-Anhalt is lower than in most other German states, the number of foreigners there has roughly quadrupled in little more than a decade, to 192,000 in 2025 from 47,000 in 2014, according to state statistics. Nearly all have the legal right to stay under federal law, and roughly a third are refugees, mostly from Syria and Ukraine.

That rise has jolted this state of 2.1 million people, which had historically experienced lower immigration than other parts of Germany and where unemployment is especially high.

Residents feared immigrants were taking their jobs, even though experts said foreign workers could help fill a chronic shortage of skilled labor. Opposition intensified after a Saudi doctor drove an S.U.V. into a Christmas market in Magdeburg in 2024, killing six people.

Michael Penther, 67, a retiree and AfD supporter from Magdeburg, said he backed the party because he believed that immigrants were fomenting crime. According to state statistics, crime has fallen in Saxony-Anhalt since 2014. But the proportion of crimes that asylum seekers and undocumented immigrants in Saxony-Anhalt were suspected of committing in 2025, excluding violations of immigration law, was disproportionately high compared with their share of the population.

Some immigrants were skeptical that the AfD would have much of an effect on immigrants with legal status who work, pay taxes and abide by the law.

Rahimi Qabilshaha, 35, a security worker, said he came to Germany in 2021 after the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan. He said the AfD had made campaign promises that it would find hard to fulfill in power.

“We will wait and see what policies the AfD adopts toward immigrants in the future,” he said. “We will then decide whether the AfD can be considered a good party for immigrants or not.”

Yet for refugees who have not yet obtained legal status, the election result is “a panic situation,” said Krzysztof Blau, who runs One World House, a migrant rights association that hosted the election night watch party.

Even the house’s future is uncertain. Founded in response to right-wing attacks on foreigners in 1994, it is a beacon for migrants, providing offices to nonprofits that offer legal and social aid. Almost 30 percent of its approximately $2.6 million annual budget comes from the state of Saxony-Anhalt. If the AfD takes power and withdraws funding, Mr. Blau said, the house would be forced to close in January.

Whatever the AfD ultimately does in office, some immigrants said their daily experience was already changing for the worse.

Two days before the election, Mr. Traore, the social worker, said he was at a shopping center handing out fliers for a Roman Catholic initiative urging voters to reject the AfD when he was approached by a group of boys on bicycles. Mr. Traore said one pointed at him and shouted, “Deportation!”

“It’s a pity,” Mr. Traore said. “He is a child.”

A Syrian barber said fewer customers were coming by his once-buzzing shop since he closed its doors for half a day as part of a shopkeepers’ protest against exclusion and racism. After 10 years in Magdeburg, the barber said, he is considering moving to another German state. He asked to remain anonymous out of fear of losing his remaining clients.

Whitney Chitemamwise, who arrived from Zimbabwe four years ago to complete her master's degree, said she worried about the AfD’s plan to segregate the children of asylum seekers into refugee-only schools. Though she is not an asylum seeker, she feared such a policy would cause her 2-year-old son to be mistreated because he is Black.

She said a man had recently shouted at her in a supermarket, demanding that she go back to her country. It wasn’t the first time she had been targeted, she said, but unlike before, no one stood up for her.

“It’s really not about them being in power,” she said of the AfD. “It just makes life difficult here. It makes it hard to raise a family.”

Jim Tankersley contributed reporting from Berlin.
